title: How Audience Testing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss audience testing (test screenings) in the film industry: how studios use free screenings and comment cards, the 'would you recommend to a friend' score, the origins of National Research Group (NRG) out of Apocalypse Now focus groups, and famous movies changed after test screenings (Licensed to Kill, Pretty Woman, Fatal Attraction, Scott Pilgrim, Pretty in Pink, Sunset Boulevard, Heathers, Blade Runner, Goodfellas). Also includes off-topic banter about Ron Howard, Robert Altman, Tom Cruise, Trolls 2, and a listener mail letter about commuting and missing episodes.
topics: would recommend to a friend score
Tom Cruise Mission Impossible III test screening
Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and Ron Howard on test screenings
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about movie-centric episodes, a spoiler warning, and introduce audience testing. Ron Howard and Brian Grazer describe testing as useful but unpleasant; Robert Altman is mentioned as a filmmaker who would resist it.

segments.title: Test screenings history and famous cuts
segments.summary: Discussion of Ron Howard's view of testing, a tangent on Robert Altman and movies such as Nashville and The Player, and the note that studios tested films as far back as the 1930s, including the cut of Somewhere Over the Rainbow that was kept in The Wizard of Oz.

segments.title: Apocalypse Now focus groups and National Research Group
segments.summary: Hosts describe focus groups for Apocalypse Now, where Joe Farrell was hired for marketing and partnered with Katherine Carr to form National Research Group, which signed studios to exclusive audience-testing contracts. NRG is described as a secretive Nielsen division.

segments.title: Audience demographics and four quadrants
segments.summary: Companies also phoned people for awareness campaigns. Audiences are split into four quadrants by gender and age under or over 25, with the 18-to-34 group being the sweet spot.

segments.title: Testing comedies and violence
segments.summary: Testing is useful for comedy jokes and pacing, but questioning of exact violence levels is discussed. Goodfellas is cited as an example: it was Scorsese's first tested movie, and audiences walked out during violence and disliked the drawn-out third act and ending.

segments.title: How recruitment and screenings work
segments.summary: Clipboard recruiters approach people in Los Angeles malls and movie lines to offer free screenings; LA-area residents are more often asked, and people on the film crew attend. Assistant editors scramble to temp in music and effects, and a moderator introduces the film.

segments.title: Comment cards and focus group follow-up
segments.summary: Audiences are told rough effects are unfinished and that pacing is the focus. They fill out comment cards with questions about characters, jokes, flow and favorite parts. Some are invited to a follow-up focus group.

segments.title: Would recommend to a friend score
segments.summary: The key metric is whether viewers say they would definitely recommend the movie to a friend; only definite yeses count toward the score, and scores above about 80 are considered decent.
topics: would recommend to a friend score

segments.title: Bad movies and Tom Cruise crashing a test screening
segments.summary: Hosts wonder how poorly reviewed films got released and mention Human Centipede 3. They say Tom Cruise crashed a Mission: Impossible III test screening, which undermines honest feedback. Banter follows about an LA Weekly article and Scientology.

segments.title: Going Clear and off-topic banter
segments.summary: Brief tangent about the HBO documentary Going Clear, based on the Lawrence Wright book, and its legal vetting.

segments.title: Famous title and ending changes: Licensed to Kill, Pretty Woman, Fatal Attraction
segments.summary: Licensed to Kill was originally called License Revoked, changed after American test audiences were confused. Pretty Woman was originally titled 3000 and had a darker ending in script form, which Gary Marshall changed. The Fatal Attraction ending, where Glenn Close's character kills herself and Michael Douglas is framed, was changed after test audiences disliked her, so she is killed off instead.

segments.title: Scott Pilgrim, Pretty in Pink, 28 Days Later, Sunset Boulevard
segments.summary: Scott Pilgrim's test audiences rejected Ramona Flowers losing to Knives, so the ending was changed and then restored to match the graphic novel. Pretty in Pink originally had Molly Ringwald end with Duckie. 28 Days Later's original ending had Cillian Murphy die. Sunset Boulevard originally opened with Holden's corpse narrating in the morgue, which audiences found comedic, and Billy Wilder reshot it as a voiceover.

segments.title: Heathers and Blade Runner endings
segments.summary: Heathers' original script ending had Veronica blow up the school with Christian Slater's character dead; the released version has her shoot him. Blade Runner's original dark ending was replaced by a studio-added voiceover and a happy ending with stock footage of blue sky from The Shining outtakes, while the director's cut is more ambiguous.

segments.title: Wrap-up and Mental Floss credit
segments.summary: Hosts credit Mental Floss for much of the list material and invite listeners to join a test audience and search for audience testing on the website.

segments.title: Listener mail: commuting and missing an oceans episode
segments.summary: Andrew writes that he switched from a Brooklyn-to-Manhattan train commute to biking to work in Brooklyn, so he now misses episodes; he missed key points in the oceans episode about riptides and equatorial winds. Hosts respond lightly.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and close the episode.
